## Web Development Company in Pune: Getting a Business App Approved on the Apple App Store — The Review Rules That Cause Rejections, Explained Before You Pay for the Build

An iPhone app is approved or rejected against Apple's App Review Guidelines, and a handful of those rules cause most of the avoidable rejections for ordinary business apps: the app being too close to a repackaged website, no working demo account for the reviewer, selling digital features without Apple's in-app purchase, offering sign-in with another service without a privacy-respecting alternative, accounts that cannot be deleted inside the app, and a missing privacy policy or support contact. None of these is hard to satisfy if it is planned at the start, and all of them are expensive to fix after the build is finished. This guide is for a business owner, clinic, school, retailer or non-profit in Pune or elsewhere in India that is considering an iOS app, and for the developer or agency quoting for it. It walks through the guidelines that matter most, what each means for a typical business app, how to prepare the submission, and what to ask your vendor before you sign.

We rely on Apple's App Review Guidelines, quoting the sections cited. Apple updates the guidelines from time to time, and the page we read was long enough that we reviewed only the sections relevant to business apps; always check the current text before you submit. We do not state approval rates, review times or fees, because we have not sourced them here, and they change. Where a point is our own practice, we say so.

## Start with the question Apple will ask: why is this an app?

Section 4.2, "Minimum Functionality", says the app "should include features, content, and UI that elevate it beyond a repackaged website" and that an app that is "not particularly useful, unique, or 'app-like'" does not belong on the App Store. Section 4.2.2 adds that other than catalogs, apps "shouldn't primarily be marketing materials, advertisements, web clippings, content aggregators, or a collection of links."

Read that with your own plan in mind. A business that wraps its existing website in an app shell, with no extra capability, is the textbook case for this rejection. The question to answer before you commission anything is what the app will do that the website cannot do as well. Genuinely app-like features include things a phone does well: push notifications for orders or appointments, a saved account with history, a camera used for a real purpose such as uploading a prescription or a document, offline access to a booked ticket, or a loyalty card that works at the counter. Whether your business needs any of these is a business question, and our article on [mobile app versus website](/blog/web-development-company-pune-mobile-app-vs-website-2026/) helps you weigh it. If the honest answer is that a good website serves your customers, the right decision may be not to build an app at all.

Section 4.2.3(i) adds a point that matters for bundled services: the app "should work on its own without requiring installation of another app to function."

## The rules that decide most business-app reviews

### Completeness and the demo account (Guideline 2.1)

Section 2.1 says submissions "should be final versions with all necessary metadata and fully functional URLs included; placeholder text, empty websites, and other temporary content should be scrubbed before submission." It also says to "include demo account info (and turn on your back-end service!) if your app includes a login." If a demo account is not possible because of legal or security obligations, the guideline allows a built-in demo mode, but with prior approval from Apple.

For a business app this means three practical things. First, prepare a reviewer account that works end to end, with sample data such as a pre-filled order history or a booked appointment, so that the reviewer can see every feature. Second, keep your server running and reachable during review; a reviewer who sees an error because a staging server was switched off will reject the build. Third, scrub placeholder text, test products and dummy links before you submit. Section 2.1(b) adds that if you offer in-app purchases, they must be complete, visible to the reviewer and functional, and if any configured item cannot be found, you should explain why in the review notes.

### Payments: when you must use Apple's in-app purchase, and when you must not (Guideline 3.1)

This is the section that most often surprises Indian businesses, because the answer depends on what you sell.

Section 3.1.1 says that if you want to unlock features or functionality within the app, with subscriptions, premium content or unlocking a full version given as examples, "you must use in-app purchase." It also says apps may not use their own mechanisms to unlock content or functionality, such as license keys, QR codes or cryptocurrency.

But section 3.1.3(e) says that if the app enables people to purchase physical goods or services that will be consumed outside of the app, you "must use purchase methods other than in-app purchase to collect those payments, such as Apple Pay or traditional credit card entry." So an online store selling garments, an electrician-booking app, a grocery delivery app or a restaurant ordering app collects payment through a normal payment gateway, not through in-app purchase. Section 3.1.3(d) covers real-time person-to-person services such as tutoring, medical consultations or fitness training between two individuals, where other purchase methods may be used; it says one-to-few and one-to-many real-time services must use in-app purchase. Section 3.1.3(f) covers free stand-alone companion apps for a paid web-based tool, such as cloud storage, email or web hosting, which need not use in-app purchase provided there is no purchasing inside the app, or calls to action for purchase outside of it.

What this means in practice: classify what you sell before you design the checkout. A coaching institute selling video courses to be watched in the app is selling digital content, which points to in-app purchase. A clinic taking payment for a consultation with one doctor is closer to the person-to-person case. A store selling physical goods uses a gateway. Where your product sits on a boundary, ask Apple through the review notes or the developer support route rather than guessing. This classification affects what Apple takes and how you build, so it belongs in the quotation stage; we do not state Apple's commission rates here because we have not sourced them for this article, and you should confirm them in Apple's current programme documentation. For the website-side payment integration, see our [payment gateway service](/services/payment-gateway/).

Subscriptions have their own rules in section 3.1.2(a): the subscription period must last at least seven days and be available across all of the user's devices, and subscribers should be able to get what they have paid for without additional tasks. Apps that trick users into subscribing are removed.

### Login: Sign in with another service (Guideline 4.8)

Section 4.8 says that if an app uses a third-party or social login as the primary account login, it must also offer an equivalent login service that limits data collection to name and email, allows the user to keep their email address private, and does not collect interactions with the app for advertising without consent. Exceptions apply: you do not need it if the app exclusively uses your company's own account setup and sign-in systems, if it is an education, enterprise or business app that requires an existing education or enterprise account, or if it uses a government or industry-backed citizen identification system.

For a small business, the simplest route is often to offer your own login with email or phone OTP, which falls under the first exception. If you want "Continue with Google" for convenience, plan to add the privacy-respecting alternative that the guideline describes. Decide this at the design stage, because adding a second login service late in the build touches the account system, the database and the testing.

### Data collection, privacy policy and account deletion (Guideline 5.1.1)

Section 5.1.1(i) says all apps must include a link to their privacy policy in the App Store Connect metadata field and within the app in an easily accessible manner. The policy must explain the app's data retention and deletion policies and describe how a user can revoke consent or request deletion of their data. Section 5.1.1(ii) says paid functionality must not depend on a user granting access to data, and that apps must provide an easy way to withdraw consent. Section 5.1.1(iii) is data minimisation: only request access to data relevant to the core functionality, and only collect what is required for the task.

Section 5.1.1(v) says that if the app does not include significant account-based features, people should be able to use it without a login. If the app supports account creation, you must also "offer account deletion within the app." The same section says the app may not require personal information to function, except when directly relevant to the core functionality or required by law. Section 5.1.1(x) lets an app ask for basic contact details, such as name and email, so long as the request is optional and features are not conditional on providing them.

The practical consequences are straightforward. Do not force registration before the user can browse your catalogue or read your information. Build a working "delete my account" option inside the app, not a request to email support. Write a privacy policy that matches what the app actually collects, and link it in two places. Our article on the [DPDP consent framework](/blog/crm-dpdp-consent-manager-framework-india-2026/) covers the Indian data-protection side of the same obligations, which is a separate legal question from Apple's rules and needs its own attention.

### Contact information (Guideline 1.5)

Section 1.5 says people need to know how to reach you with questions and support issues, and that your app and its Support URL should include an easy way to contact you. It adds that failing to include accurate and up-to-date contact information may violate the law in some countries or regions. A support page with a real email address and phone number, and an in-app link to it, satisfies this. A contact form that goes nowhere does not.

## Preparing the submission: a practical checklist

This is our own working checklist, built from the sections above. It is a practice, not a list issued by Apple.

1. **Write the app's purpose in one sentence** that explains why it is more than a website. If you cannot, revisit the plan before building.
2. **Classify what you sell** against sections 3.1.1 and 3.1.3 and record the answer.
3. **Decide the login method** against section 4.8.
4. **Build account deletion inside the app** if accounts exist.
5. **Prepare the privacy policy** and link it in App Store Connect and in the app.
6. **Create a reviewer demo account** with realistic data, and confirm the back end is live.
7. **Remove placeholder content**, test data and dead links.
8. **Set a support URL and contact details** that work.
9. **Test on real devices** and on slow connections, including the first-run experience a reviewer will see.
10. **Write review notes** that explain the demo account, how to reach the main features, and anything unusual, such as why a payment is not an in-app purchase.
11. **Plan for a rejection.** Even careful submissions are sometimes returned with questions. Budget time and a fix window in the project plan rather than treating the first submission as the launch date.

A worked example, illustrative only and not a client result. A Pune bakery wants an app for ordering cakes. The website already lets customers browse and order. The app's purpose sentence is: "Reorder a previous cake in two taps, track the delivery with notifications, and save addresses and photos of custom designs." Cakes are physical goods consumed outside the app, so payment goes through a normal gateway under section 3.1.3(e). Login is the bakery's own phone-number OTP, so section 4.8 is not triggered. Account deletion is built into the profile screen. The reviewer account has a saved address and a past order. That plan answers the likely questions before they are asked.

## Account, fees and timing: what we cannot tell you here

To publish, you need an Apple Developer Program membership and an App Store Connect account. We have not sourced current fees, enrolment requirements for organisations in India, or typical review times for this article, and they change, so confirm them on Apple's developer site before budgeting. As a matter of ownership, we would insist that the developer account is registered in your business's name and not the agency's, for the same reasons set out in our [website handover and ownership checklist](/blog/web-development-company-pune-website-handover-ownership-checklist-2026/). If the agency owns the account, you may find that you cannot move the app to another provider without losing the listing and its reviews.

If you are planning for both platforms, our article on [launching on Google Play](/blog/web-development-company-pune-google-play-launch-closed-testing-target-api-2026/) covers the Android side, and our comparison of [Flutter and React Native](/blog/web-development-company-pune-flutter-react-native-mobile-apps-2026/) helps with the technology choice, since both platforms' review rules should be considered together. Do not forget what happens after launch: operating systems change, libraries need updates, and apps that are not maintained can be affected. Our guide to [mobile app maintenance cost](/blog/web-development-company-pune-mobile-app-maintenance-cost-2026/) sets out what to budget.

## Questions to ask a vendor before you sign

- Why does this need to be an app rather than a website, and what will it do that the website cannot?
- How do the payment and subscription rules in section 3.1 apply to what we sell, and how will the checkout be built?
- Which login method will we use, and does section 4.8 apply?
- Will account deletion be built into the app?
- Who will own the Apple Developer account and the App Store Connect listing?
- Who prepares the demo account and the review notes, and who pays for resubmissions if Apple asks for changes?
- Does the quotation include maintenance after launch, or is that separate?

A vendor who has shipped apps before will answer these quickly. A vendor who has not will tell you that approval is "guaranteed", which no one can promise.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### Why do Apple App Store reviews reject business apps?

Common reasons from Apple's guidelines include an app that is only a repackaged website, no working demo account for the reviewer, placeholder content, selling digital features without in-app purchase, a missing privacy policy, offering third-party login without an equivalent privacy-respecting option, and no way to delete an account inside the app.

### Do I have to use Apple's in-app purchase for my business app?

It depends on what you sell. Apple's section 3.1.1 requires in-app purchase for unlocking features or digital content, while section 3.1.3(e) says physical goods or services consumed outside the app must use other payment methods such as Apple Pay or card entry. Real-time one-to-one services have their own exception in 3.1.3(d).

### Do I need to let users delete their account in the app?

Yes, if the app supports account creation. Section 5.1.1(v) says you must offer account deletion within the app. It also says that if the app has no significant account-based features, people should be able to use it without a login.

### Can I just turn my website into an iPhone app?

Apple's section 4.2 says an app should include features, content and UI that elevate it beyond a repackaged website, and 4.2.2 says apps should not primarily be marketing materials, links or web clippings other than catalogs. A bare website wrapper is at risk of rejection.

### Do I need a demo account for Apple's reviewers?

If your app has a login, yes. Section 2.1 says to include demo account information and turn on your back-end service. A built-in demo mode is allowed only with prior approval from Apple.
